PROJECT NO. 58777


TEXAS PUBLIC POLICY FOUNDATION'S RESPONSES TO STAFF QUESTIONS

TO THE HONORABLE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:

The Texas Public Policy Foundation (TPPF or the Foundation), through its Life:Powered campaign, respectfully submits the following comments in response to staff’s questions regarding ERCOT’s assumptions for the 2026 reliability assessment, as required by 16 TAC §25.508.

TPPF believes that this assessment is critical because the winter resource adequacy situation has continued to deteriorate since Winter Storm Uri, even as the operational performance of the grid during winter storms has improved. Using consistent methodologies to account for both generation and demand during the winter peak hours (ERCOT has changed the methods in its MORA reports multiple times, especially its peak demand forecasts), our research shows that the winter reserve margin in ERCOT has declined from 17.5% in 2021 to about 10% in 2026 and could easily be negative by 2030. This fact is not well-known among policymakers and even among many market participants. ERCOT and the Commission need to use this opportunity to provide a thorough and uniform set of data and forecasts that stakeholders can use to assess the future of the ERCOT grid and potential policy changes.

The manner which the ERCOT market is continuing to meet new demand growth primarily with solar and energy storage is increasing the system’s vulnerability to a long-duration winter storm. Prior to Winter Storm Uri, nearly $100 billion was invested primarily in new wind energy in Texas. Investing just a quarter of that amount in new reliable generation, weatherization, etc. would have significantly reduced the extent of outages during the storm. Since Uri, this pattern has continued, with over $50 billion being invested in 31 GW of new solar, 17 GW of storage, and 11 GW of wind. Just 3 GW of new gas generation has been built during that time. This situation is likely to continue for the next few years, with solar and storage comprising more than 80% of projects in the later stages of the interconnection queue.

It is not a sign of failure if the market drives investment into solar and storage to some degree, but to invest in those resources almost exclusively and to rely on them for winter resource adequacy is a serious deficiency. Our projections show that even with a conservative forecast of data center uptake to the grid, the ERCOT region is likely to fall short of the reliability standard by all three measures—frequency, duration, and magnitude—by the winter of 2030. The only way to mitigate the problem is through greater uptake of reliable generation to the grid and flexibility from data centers during peak demand periods.

Regarding policy changes, §25.508(c)(3)(C) requires ERCOT to “provide the commission with a menu of proposed recommended market design changes” if “the assessment shows that any reviewed system fails to meet the reliability standard.” The Foundation hopes and expects that ERCOT will fulfill this requirement to the best of its ability and continue to initiate discussions on this important matter. In addition to proposing new programs, ERCOT should also consider the efficacy of modifying existing programs such as the firming reliability requirement or the Dispatchable Reliability Reserve Service to tie them more directly to the needs identified in the reliability assessment.

Given the complexity and the quickly evolving nature of the winter reliability situation in the ERCOT region, the Foundation appreciates the Commission’s efforts to guide a robust discussion on ERCOT’s reliability assessment. We offer the following comments in response to the staff’s questions.

Questions 1(a) and (b)

TPPF agrees with the broad consensus that the current CONE is already out of date and should be updated before assessing any market reform proposals, with the caveat that it can be done while still hewing to the late Q3 2026 timeframe for delivering the reliability assessment and proposed market reforms. Given the proposal to accomplish this task by mid-May, TPPF supports moving forward with that study. The scope of the study and list of tasks seems reasonable, and TPPF does not have any suggestions to amend that.

Questions 2(a) and (b)

TPPF supports updating the load forecast in accordance with the 2026 RTP as long as the resulting delay is brief. Our work assessing different winter reliability scenarios shows how sensitive the reliability assessment is to future load growth and the importance of an accurate forecast. As the ERCOT market increasingly relies on energy storage for resource adequacy, even a 5 GW shift in demand up or down, spread out over 24 hours or more, can make a significant difference in the amount of unserved energy during a long-duration winter storm. Our opinion is that even ERCOT’s adjusted load forecast likely overestimates the amount of load that will connect to the grid in the next 3 to 4 years given the existing constraints on the transmission system and that a more conservative forecast, perhaps including a significant amount of demand flexibility, is warranted.

If the delay is expected to be more than a month, then TPPF would not support using an updated forecast. Although accuracy is important, delivery of the assessment before the end of the calendar year and the beginning of the 2027 legislative session is of paramount importance. The situation on the ground is changing so rapidly that even the best load forecast will likely change significantly within a year’s time, and we cannot let the good be defeated in search of the perfect in this effort.

Question 3(a)

In our view, ERCOT’s CDR Report does a good job estimating capacity additions up to two years into the future, but beyond that point, it tends to underestimate capacity additions. To that end, we recommend that the assessment include several additional GW each of wind, solar, and storage capacity beyond what is in the CDR, as well as a few GW of new gas, consistent with the current resource trends.

Question 4(a)

TPPF agrees with the magnitude values in ERCOT’s proposed assumptions.

Questions 5(a) and (b)

TPPF has no comment on the proposed gas and coal price assumptions except to suggest that a sensitivity analysis be performed, especially a scenario with significantly higher prices that considers possible supply shocks and significant increases in the exports of both commodities over the next few years.

Questions 6(a) and (b)

TPPF has no comment on these questions at this time.

Questions 7(a) and (b)

TPPF has no comment on these questions at this time.

Question 8(a)

TPPF has no comment on this question at this time.

Questions 9(a) and 9(b)

As the ERCOT grid relies more on wind and solar for winter resource adequacy, the quantity and type of winter precipitation could be just as important as temperature to future winter reliability. During Winter Storm Fern, which primarily brought sleet across most of the state instead of freezing rain or snow, over 13 GW of nameplate wind capacity, about a third of the entire fleet, was out for the duration of the storm. The availability of those resources also impacts energy storage availability during a long-duration storm. Recent winter storms have also demonstrated the impact of winter precipitation on both transmission availability and demand. Therefore, TPPF requests that ERCOT incorporate precipitation into the probabilistic weather impacts in addition to temperature. If ERCOT cannot do so in a timely manner now, then we hope precipitation is considered in future studies.

Question 10

TPPF has no further comments on other model assumptions and commends PUC staff for undertaking a thorough assessment of ERCOT’s assumptions.
PROJECT NO. 58777


COMMENTS OF THE TEXAS PUBLIC POLICY FOUNDATION: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

While the winter operational performance of the ERCOT grid has markedly improved since Winter Storm Uri, the quantity of firm generation available has not risen in concert with winter demand, which has led to a growing winter capacity gap.
TPPF’s projections show that even with a conservative forecast of data center uptake to the grid, the ERCOT region is likely to fall short of the reliability standard by all three measures—frequency, duration, and magnitude—by the winter of 2030. The only way to mitigate the problem is through greater uptake of reliable generation to the grid and flexibility from data centers during peak demand periods.
ERCOT should be prepared to offer multiple options to mitigate the winter reliability deficit and to drive discussions on market design changes. In addition to proposing new programs, ERCOT should also consider the efficacy of modifying existing programs such as the firming reliability requirement or the Dispatchable Reliability Reserve Service to tie them more directly to the needs identified in the reliability assessment.
TPPF supports updating both the CONE and the load forecasts prior to performing this assessment if those changes can be made while hewing to the plan to publish the reliability assessment by the end of Q3 2026. While the accuracy of the assessment is important, and accurate assumptions are essential for accurate outputs, the rapidly evolution of the grid right now means that any assumptions derived this year will change considerably within a year’s time. Timely delivery of the assessment is paramount to accuracy right now.
With the growth of wind and solar, the quantity and type of winter precipitation is becoming nearly as important as temperature for determining winter demand and generation availability. ERCOT should consider ways to incorporate a sensitivity analysis regarding winter precipitation in this study or at a minimum to begin developing methods to do so in future studies.
